content: Britches was the name given to a stump-tailed macaque monkey born in March 1985 at a breeding colony at the University of California, Riverside. Immediately after birth, he was separated from his mother and subjected to a maternal and sensory deprivation study. His eyelids were surgically sewn shut as part of a three-year experiment involving 24 infant monkeys. This study, led by researcher David H. Warren, aimed to investigate the behavioral and neural development of monkeys raised with sensory substitution devices. At five weeks old, Britches was rescued during a raid conducted by the Animal Liberation Front (ALF) on April 20, 1985. During the raid, ALF removed 700 animals from the laboratory, including Britches. A videotape documenting the raid and Britches' condition was later released by People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA). The footage revealed the state in which Britches was found, leading to widespread public condemnation of the experiments. Prominent organizations, including the American Council of the Blind, criticized the study. Dr. Grant Mack, president of the American Council of the Blind, described the experiment as one of the most repugnant and ill-conceived boondoggles he had encountered. The experiments were designed to study the effects of sensory deprivation and the use of a sensory substitution device called the Trisensor Aid (TSA), an experimental version of a blind travel aid known as the Sonicguide. Five groups of four macaques were to be raised from birth to three months, with one group raised to six months. Some monkeys were blinded and fitted with the TSA, while others served as control groups with normal vision or wore a dummy device. At the conclusion of the study, the monkeys were to be euthanized, and their brains examined for changes in visual, auditory, and motor areas. Veterinarian reports from the ALF raid described Britches' condition as distressing. He was found alone in a cage with bandages around his eyes and a sonar device attached to his head, which emitted high-pitched screeches at intervals. He clung to a surrogate mother device covered in toweling with two fake nipples attached. Dr. Ned Buyukmihci, a veterinary ophthalmologist from the University of California, Davis, examined Britches and reported that the sutures used to sew his eyelids shut were excessively large and poorly executed, causing lacerations to the eyelids. The eye pads were filthy and soaked with moisture. Dr. Buyukmihci stated, There is no possible justification for this sloppy, painful experiment. Another veterinarian, Bettina Flavioli, hired by the ALF, also examined Britches and documented his condition, noting severe inflammation, poor muscle development, dry skin, and a foul body odor. Following the raid, eight of the 17 interrupted studies were not resumed, and the university ceased allowing baby monkeys' eyes to be sewn shut. Britches was later flown to a sanctuary in Mexico, where he was cared for by an elderly female macaque who had previously raised several orphaned monkeys. His story inspired a Spanish rock band, Lyvon, to dedicate a song to him titled Cry Britches (Llora Britches). The song and its accompanying video honored both Britches and the efforts of the Animal Liberation Front, highlighting the fight against animal mistreatment and the liberation of animals from such conditions.
